17   II.  LEGAL STANDARD                                                   
18        As this action is premised on federal question jurisdiction, federal common law governs 
19   issues of privilege.  Fed. R. Evid. 501; United States v. Ruehle, 583 F.3d 600, 608 (9th Cir. 2009). 
20        “The attorney-client privilege protects confidential communications between attorneys and 
21   clients, which are made for the purpose of giving legal advice.”  United States v. Sanmina Corp., 
22   968 F.3d 1107, 1116 (9th Cir. 2020).  The privilege extends to a client’s confidential disclosures 
23   to an attorney in order to obtain legal advice, as well as an attorney’s advice in response to such 
24   disclosures.  Ruehle, 583 F.3d at 607 (citations and quotations omitted). “Because it impedes full 
25   and free discovery of the truth, the attorney-client privilege is strictly construed.”  Id. (citations 
26   and quotations omitted).                                              
27        In the Ninth Circuit, whether information is protected by the attorney-client privilege is

              the legal adviser, (8) unless the protection be waived.

4   Sanmina, 968 F.3d at 1116.  Where a communication has more than one purpose, it may be 
5   protected as privileged if the primary purpose of the communication is to give or receive legal 
6   advice, as opposed to business or some other non-legal advice.  In re Grand Jury, 13 F.4th 710, 
7   714 (9th Cir. 2021) (describing and adopting the “primary purpose” test for dual-purpose 
8   communications).                                                      
9        The party asserting attorney-client privilege bears the burden of proving that the privilege 
10   applies.  Ruehle, 583 F.3d at 608.                                    
11   III.  DISCUSSION                                                      
12        Plaintiffs challenge Meta’s clawback of the disputed communications on three grounds.  
13   First, plaintiffs argue that the communications are not privileged because they were not made for 
14   the purpose of giving legal advice.  Second, plaintiffs argue that the communications were not 
15   made in confidence between an attorney and client because Ms. Hanh, a non-employee, was a 
16   party to each communication.  Third, plaintiffs argue that Meta waived any privilege over these 
17   communications by producing them in unredacted form to the FTC.  The Court considers each 
18   argument.                                                             
19        A.   Purpose of the Redacted Communications                      
20        Plaintiffs do not have access to the disputed communications.  However, based on the 
21   unredacted portions of the April 8-9, 2018 email exchange, plaintiffs argue that the 
22   communications were made for the purpose of providing public relations support in response to an 
23   inquiry from the press—i.e., for a business purpose, and not for the purpose of giving or receiving 
24   legal advice.  Dkt. No. 195-1 at ECF 12.  They point out that the email exchange begins with an 
25   inquiry from a TechCrunch journalist to a Meta communications manager about Meta’s data 
26   access policies, and is followed shortly thereafter by an email from the communications manager 
27   to all others in the email exchange attaching a copy of the published article and stating:  “Here’s

4   litigation.  In particular, Meta’s response to criticism that its conduct was “anti-competitive” and 
5   “hurts users” would have legal implications for Meta.  Dkt. No. 198 at 6.  Meta notes that, as a 
6   general matter, it coordinates its response to press inquiries with its legal team because the 
7   company’s public statements may be deemed admissions in litigation, and it says this concern was

13   unredacted portions of the email exchange.  Based on that review, as well as a careful

17   While some of the disputed communications include information that might be considered factual 
18   and therefore not privileged, including a description of other companies’ policies and references to 
19   Meta’s prior public statements about its own policies, the disputed communications as a whole 
20   concern the giving and receiving of legal advice regarding Meta’s response to the press inquiry.  
21   See Upjohn Co. v. United States, 449 U.S. 383, 395-96 (1981) (“A fact is one thing and a 
22   communication concerning that fact is an entirely different thing.”) (quotations and citation

26   does not appear that privileged information was included merely to prevent disclosure of non-
27   privileged matters.”).  Of course, the underlying facts about how Meta handled data access issues

5        B.   Ms. Hahn’s Role                                             
6        Plaintiffs argue that even if the disputed communications concern legal advice, they are not 
7   privileged because they were not made in confidence.  Dkt. No. 188 at 10.  They note that Ms. 
8   Hanh, who was copied on all such communications, was not a Meta employee and is therefore 
9   outside the attorney-client relationship.  Id.  Meta acknowledges that Ms. Hanh was not employed 
10   by Meta at the time of the email exchange, but it argues that she was a “functional employee” of 
11   Meta and that her inclusion in the email exchange does not destroy the privilege.  Dkt. No. 198 at 
12   8.                                                                    
13        Generally, an attorney-client communication made in the presence of, or shared with, a 
14   third party is not confidential and therefore not privileged.  See Nidec Corp. v. Victor Co. of 
15   Japan, 249 F.R.D. 575, 578 (N.D. Cal. 2007).  However, in United States v. Graf, the Ninth 
16   Circuit held that where a third party is the functional equivalent of a corporate employee, her 
17   participation or inclusion in an attorney-client communication does not destroy the corporation’s 
18   privilege.  Graf, 610 F.3d 1148, 1158-59 (9th Cir. 2010) (citing In re Bieter Co., 16 F.3d 929 (8th 
19   Cir. 1994)).                                                          
20        Graf adopted the reasoning of the Eighth Circuit in In re Bieter Co.  In that case, the 
21   Eighth Circuit found that the privilege applied to communications between corporate counsel and 
22   an outside consultant who “was in all relevant respects the functional equivalent of an employee” 
23   because he was “involved on a daily basis with the principals of Bieter and on Bieter’s behalf in 
24   the unsuccessful development that serve[d] as the basis for th[e] litigation,” and because “his 
25   involvement in the subject of the litigation make him precisely the sort of person with whom a 
26   lawyer would wish to confer confidentially in order to understand Bieter’s reasons for seeking 
27   representation.”  In re Bieter Co., 16 F.3d at 938.  The Eighth Circuit observed that, in that case, 
1   that it was therefore “inappropriate to distinguish between those on the client’s payroll and those 
2   who are instead, and for whatever reason, employed as independent contractors.”  Id. at 937. 
3        In Graf, the Ninth Circuit affirmed a district court’s finding that a criminal defendant who 
4   was a consultant to insurance company engaged in a health insurance fraud scheme was an agent 
5   of the company, such that his communications with the company’s counsel fell within the 
6   company’s attorney-client privilege.  Graf, 610 F.3d at 1159.  In concluding that the 
7   defendant/consultant was a functional employee of the insurance company, the Ninth Circuit noted 
8   that he “regularly communicated with insurance brokers and others on behalf of [the company], 
9   marketed the company’s insurance plans, managed its employees, and was the company’s voice in 
10   its communications with counsel.”  Id. at 1158.  In addition, the Ninth Circuit observed that the 
11   defendant likely was a consultant to the company only because he could not legally be employed 
12   by an insurance company in the State of California, but that “his actual role” was the functional 
13   equivalent of an employee, officer, or director.  Id. at 1157-59.     
14        Underlying the decisions in Graf and In re Bieter Co. is the Supreme Court’s holding in 
15   Upjohn Co. v. United States that “a corporation’s privilege extends to communications between 
16   corporate employees and corporate counsel as long as the communications are made at the 
17   direction of corporate superiors in order to secure legal advice.”  Graf, 610 F.3d at 1158 (internal 
18   quotations omitted) (citing Upjohn, 449 U.S. at 390-94).  In rejecting the narrower “control group” 
19   test, Upjohn held that the scope of the privilege must be assessed based on understanding which 
20   employees possess the information needed by the corporation’s counsel to enable the giving of 
21   legal advice, as well as which employees are responsible for acting on that advice.  Upjohn, 449 
22   U.S. at 390-392.  Upjohn left unresolved the question of when communications with a person who 
23   is not a corporate employee might fall within the scope of the corporation’s attorney-client 
24   privilege.  In adopting the Eighth Circuit’s “functional employee” analysis, the Ninth Circuit 
25   concluded that a corporation’s privilege properly encompasses communications between corporate 
26   counsel and the corporation’s non-employee representatives or consultants who have information 
27   corporate counsel needs to provide legal advice to the corporation.  See Graf, 610 F.3d at 1158-

8        C.   Unredacted Production to the FTC                            
9        Plaintiffs argue that because Meta produced the April 8-9, 2018 email exchange in 
10   unredacted form to the FTC in 2019 in response to a civil investigative demand, Meta waived any 
11   privilege that otherwise may have protected the disputed communications.  Dkt. No. 188, at 14-15.  
12   Meta responds that the Clawback Order (Dkt. No. 191) bars plaintiffs’ challenge because it 
13   permits the clawback of the disputed communications without any consideration of whether a 
14   party’s production of privileged material was inadvertent or otherwise satisfies the requirements of 
15   Federal Rule of Evidence 502(b).  Dkt. No. 198 at 11.  In addition, Meta argues that its prior 
16   production of the disputed communications to the FTC did not waive privilege given the nature of 
17   the production and the regulations that govern FTC proceedings.  Id. at 12-15. 
18        With respect to Meta’s first argument, the Clawback Order governs the treatment of 
19   “Protected Documents,” which is defined to refer to “the production or disclosure of any 
20   documents and accompanying metadata, protected from discovery[.]”  Dkt. No. 191 at 1.  The 
21   Clawback Order “governs all disputes regarding Protected Documents produced in this litigation.”  
22   Id.  As the Court explained at the hearing, the Clawback Order applies only to documents 
23   produced in discovery in this case; it does not specify the conditions for evaluating whether a prior 
24   production of documents in another proceeding resulted in a waiver of privilege, even if that prior 
25   production is subsequently re-produced to a party in this case.6  See Dkt. No. 211 at 23:6-23. 
26   Accordingly, the Court turns to the merits of plaintiffs’ argument that Meta’s prior production of
